name: Apollo 13’s third stage
intro: This crater was made by the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 13. While the crew fought to get home after an oxygen tank exploded, the empty stage hit the Moon on purpose on 15 April 1970 (14 April in Houston). It was the first rocket stage ever crashed into the Moon. Look up: the see-through rocket stage over the crater shows how it looked a moment before it hit.

hotspots.title: The crater
hotspots.text: The stage blasted out a crater about 30 meters across, wider than a basketball court is long. NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed it decades later.

source.label: LROC: Rocket impacts recorded by the Apollo seismic network

photo.alt: A grey, cratered moonscape seen from above, with one fresh crater surrounded by bright rays.
photo.caption: The crater from orbit: the bright rays are fresh soil thrown out by the crash.
photo.licenseEvidence: LROC images (NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University) are free for educational use with credit; this site is an educational NASA Space Apps project.

hotspots.title: One big engine
hotspots.text: This is the stage’s single J-2 engine. It burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen to push the Apollo ships out of Earth orbit and onto the road to the Moon.

hotspots.title: Mostly fuel tank
hotspots.text: Nearly all of the stage is fuel tank: 17.8 meters tall and 6.6 meters across, about as tall as a six-storey building. By the time it reached the Moon its fuel was used up.

hotspots.title: Steering rockets
hotspots.text: The pods on the sides hold small steering rockets. After the Apollo 13 ships pulled away, these rockets fired for 217 seconds to aim the empty stage at the Moon.

source.label: NASA NSSDCA: Apollo 13 Command and Service Module

hotspots.title: Bright rays
hotspots.text: The crash splashed fresh, light-colored soil across the darker ground, making bright streaks around the crater. Over millions of years, sunlight will slowly darken them.

source.label: LROC (LRO camera team): the Apollo S-IVB craters

hotspots.title: Felt 135 km away
hotspots.text: The Apollo 12 seismometer, about 135 km to the east, felt the ground shake. It was the only seismometer on the Moon at the time, and this crash gave it a big test signal.

source.label: LROC: Rocket impacts recorded by the Apollo seismic network

hotspots.title: Shattered stage
hotspots.text: Scout’s check: nothing is left in one piece. The 18-meter-long stage hit at about 2.6 km per second and broke into fragments scattered around the crater.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Seen from far away
hotspots.text: Scientists made this animation to show the impact as a brief flash on the dark side of the Moon, then zoom in to the real crater photographed by LRO.

source.label: NASA SVS: Apollo 13 S-IVB impact site

video.caption: Animation: the impact flashes on the night side of the Moon, then the view flies down to LRO’s real photo of the crater.

funFact: When Mission Control told the crew the stage had hit the Moon, Jim Lovell answered: “Well, at least something worked on this flight.”
whyLeft: It was used up after pushing Apollo 13 toward the Moon, and NASA chose to crash it so the new seismometers could feel a big, precisely timed thump.
repurpose: It shattered into pieces, but its aluminium is still lying around the crater. One day a Moon base could collect metal like this instead of carrying it all from Earth.
